title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
hook: a teacher warns the king that the small boy is Vishnu, and the king keeps his promise anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa began with Mahabali, the good asura king, and a small boy asking for three steps of ground. How did a day in Maveli's land go, with no small lies? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

The water pot is already tilted. In the old way of giving a gift, the giver pours water to seal the promise, and Bali is about to pour. Then his teacher, Shukra, pulls him aside. Shukra sees what the king doesn't. That small boy is Vishnu. Give him three steps and he will take everything you have. Take your word back, he says. Here, even a teacher thinks a lie would be wiser. Today, what a good king does with a promise that's about to cost him the world.
screen: `THE WATER POT TILTED` → `SHUKRA'S WARNING` → `A PROMISE THAT WILL COST`

segments.voice: First, the warning. The Bhagavata Purana gives Shukra a strong case. He tells Bali that this boy is Vishnu in disguise, and that the gift will strip him of everything. He even argues that in some moments, an untrue word is allowed. It's a teacher's counsel, and it isn't foolish. Second, the answer. Bali hears him out, and refuses. In paraphrase, he says: I am Prahlada's grandson. I have said I will give. I will not take it back. And the text puts a striking line in his mouth: the earth can carry any weight except the weight of a liar. So Bali pours the water. Shukra, angry, curses him to lose his fortune. Third, the steps. The small boy begins to grow. He grows past the sacrifice, past the trees, past the sky, until he holds the worlds inside his body. With one step he covers the earth. With the second, the heavens. And there's nowhere left for the third. Bali's own soldiers rush at the giant, and Bali stops them. He is bound with ropes. Then Vamana asks, in effect: you promised three steps, and I've taken two. Where does the third one go? And Bali answers: put it on my head. Notice what that does. He has lost his kingdom, his treasure, his freedom. The one thing he refuses to lose is his word. And he gives the last of himself, his own head, to keep it. Nobody today is asking anyone for the three worlds. But promises still get expensive halfway through. Bali's story asks what you'd hand over, and what you'd keep.
screen: `SHUKRA: TAKE YOUR WORD BACK` · `BALI: I WILL NOT` · `TWO STEPS COVER EVERYTHING` · `THE THIRD STEP ON HIS HEAD`

segments.voice: Sit with one open promise now, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open: to a friend, a child, a parent, to yourself. Don't judge it yet. Just hold it, the way Bali held the water pot. Ask quietly: what would keeping this one cost me? And what would it cost to break it? Breathe in, and let the question rest. Breathe out, and let your head bow a little, the way Bali bowed his. The bell holds the time.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Bali's choice: warned that the boy was Vishnu, he kept his word, and offered his own head for the third step. Today's word.
Your line: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, keep one small promise you'd rather slip out of, and notice what it costs. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: At Onam, Keralites retell how Mahabali kept his word to Vamana and offered his head for the third step, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of it is read and recited in the season.

fork.setup: you're Bali. your teacher says the boy is Vishnu and will take everything. the water pot is in your hands. what do you do?
options: take your word back, as your teacher says.
pour the water and keep your promise.
offer the boy a smaller gift instead.
fork.reveal: Bali keeps his word, loses the worlds in two steps, and offers his own head for the third.

original.note: Sanskrit: Trivikrama, 'of the three strides', a name of Vishnu for the giant Vamana becomes.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bali was tricked out of his kingdom.
what it means: he was warned, chose to keep his word anyway, and gave his head for the third step.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata gives Shukra a real argument for lying, so Bali's refusal is a choice, not ignorance.
recall: asked who would leave a sleeping wife
asks to see her sons once more

notes: All of today is paraphrase of the Bhagavata Purana, Skandha 8, chapters 19–22; please confirm the verse ranges cited.
Confirm the paraphrase of Bali's reply, especially the line attributed to the earth (she can bear anything but one who breaks his word, BhP 8.20.4).
Shukra's curse and the soldiers' attack follow BhP 8.20–8.21; confirm order.
The word Trivikrama for the giant form: confirm it's apt in this Bhagavata context.
Shukra (Shukracharya) is the asuras' guru; he is presented fairly, as giving reasoned counsel.
